---
title: Installation
guide-section: "Getting started"
---

trialforge targets Python 3.10+. Once it is released on PyPI:

```bash
pip install "trialforge[pl]"
```

Until then, install it from GitHub. This compiles the Rust engine from source, so it needs a Rust
toolchain (1.88 or later; [rustup](https://rustup.rs) is the easiest way to get one), and the
first build takes a few minutes:

```bash
pip install "trialforge[pl] @ git+https://github.com/rich-iannone/trialforge#subdirectory=python"
```

With uv, use `uv pip install` or `uv add` with the same requirement.

## Optional extras

The package itself has no Python dependencies. Datasets come back as DataFrames, so install a
backend with an extra; writing files needs none.

| Extra | Adds |
|---|---|
| `pl` | Polars, the default `output=` |
| `pd` | pandas (with PyArrow, which the conversion goes through) |
| `pa` | PyArrow |
| `verify`{.gd-no-link} | Pointblank, for `Study.verify(level=3)` |

Extras combine, as in `pip install "trialforge[pd,verify]"`. The DataFrame backend is imported
only when you first look at a study's datasets, so a script that only writes files runs without
any of them. If the backend for the `output=` you ask for is missing, the error names the extra
that installs it.

## Checking the installation

Import the package and generate a small study:

```{python}
import trialforge as tf

tf.study("vaccine", n=20, seed=1)
```

If that prints a study with its list of datasets, the engine works: the study was generated and
passed every check. `tf.__version__` is the package version and `tf.core_version()` the version of
the Rust engine inside it, which together identify the data a request gives (see
[Reproducibility](11-reproducibility.qmd)):

```{python}
tf.__version__, tf.core_version()
```

## Wheels

Released wheels cover Python 3.10 and later (one abi3 wheel per platform) on Linux (x86_64 and
aarch64), macOS (Intel and Apple silicon) and Windows (x86_64). Elsewhere pip builds from the
source distribution, which needs the same Rust toolchain.

## If the build fails

Installing from GitHub or from the source distribution runs a Rust build through
[maturin](https://www.maturin.rs). The usual problems are these:

- **No Rust toolchain**: the error mentions `cargo` or `rustc` not being found. Install one with
rustup, then open a new shell so that `~/.cargo/bin` is on the `PATH`.
- **An older Rust**: an error that a package "requires rustc 1.88 or newer" means the toolchain is
too old. Run `rustup update stable`.
- **No C linker**: Rust needs the platform's linker. On macOS that's the Xcode command line tools
(`xcode-select --install`), on Linux a C compiler (`build-essential` on Debian and Ubuntu), and on
Windows the "Desktop development with C++" workload of the Visual Studio Build Tools.
- **The build seems to hang**: the first build compiles the engine and its dependencies with
optimizations, which takes a few minutes. Run pip with `-v` to see its progress.
- **An old Python**: Python 3.9 and earlier aren't supported, and pip reports that no version
satisfies the requirement.

## R

The R package is built on the same engine and gives byte-identical data for the same request. See
its [documentation](../r/index.html) for installation and usage.
